questions.s: The median nerve
o: is found immediately lateral to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa

From medial to lateral the cubital fossa contains the median nerve, the brachial artery and the biceps tendon. So the median nerve lies medial to the artery, two structures medial to the tendon.
"MBBS": median, brachial, biceps (medial to lateral).
contains fibres from cervical roots 5, 6, 7 and 8 and thoracic 1

Last's gives the median nerve root value as C5 to T1, from the lateral cord (C5 to C7) and medial cord (C8, T1).
Some texts say C6 to T1.
is responsible for flexion of the distal interphalangeal joint of the little finger

The medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (ring and little fingers) is supplied by the ulnar nerve, so the median nerve does not flex the little finger DIP joint.
The anterior interosseous nerve supplies the lateral half.
is easily exposed in the arm where it is adjacent to the brachial artery by an incision along the medial border of biceps

In the arm the median nerve runs with the brachial artery along the medial bicipital groove, crossing from lateral to medial of it, so it is easily exposed through an incision along the medial border of biceps.
Answer B: 2 and 4.

questions.s: Concerning the brachial plexus:
o: The divisions lie behind the clavicle at the outer border of the first rib

The divisions of the brachial plexus lie behind the clavicle at the outer border of the first rib. Roots and trunks are supraclavicular, cords infraclavicular.
So clavicle fractures can damage the divisions.
The cords are named by their relation to the second part of the axillary artery

The cords are named by their relation to the second part of the axillary artery (behind pectoralis minor). They enter above the first part, embrace the second and give branches around the third.
Lateral, medial and posterior to the artery.
A prefixed plexus receives a major contribution from C4 and occurs in about 10%

Last's says a prefixed plexus (C4 to C8) and a postfixed plexus (C6 to T2) each occur in about 10 percent.
This affects the level of root injuries.
The lateral cord is formed by the anterior divisions of the middle and lower trunks

The lateral cord is formed by the anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks. The medial cord is the anterior division of the lower trunk.
All three posterior divisions form the posterior cord.

questions.s: Branches arising from the roots of the brachial plexus include the:
o: Suprascapular nerve

The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper trunk; it is the only branch of a trunk.
It passes through the suprascapular notch.
Dorsal scapular nerve

The dorsal scapular nerve (C5) arises from the root and passes behind the roots through scalenus medius.
It supplies the rhomboids and levator scapulae.
Lateral pectoral nerve

The lateral pectoral nerve arises from the lateral cord.
It pierces the clavipectoral fascia.
Long thoracic nerve

The long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) arises from the roots and passes behind them.
Answer B: 2 and 4.

questions.s: Regarding the root values of branches of the brachial plexus:
o: Pectoralis major is the only muscle supplied by all five roots of the plexus

Last's says pectoralis major is the only muscle supplied by all five roots of the plexus: C5 and C6 to the clavicular head, C7, C8 and T1 to the sternocostal part.
Via the lateral and medial pectoral nerves.
The thoracodorsal nerve is C6, C7 and C8

The thoracodorsal nerve (C6, C7, C8) arises from the posterior cord and supplies latissimus dorsi.
It is at risk in axillary node clearance.
The ulnar nerve receives its C7 fibres from the lateral cord in most people

Last's says in over 95 percent the ulnar nerve receives C7 fibres from the lateral cord (otherwise from the middle trunk); they supply flexor carpi ulnaris.
The "lateral root of the ulnar nerve".
The axillary nerve is C7 and C8

The axillary nerve is C5 and C6, not C7 and C8.
It is a branch of the posterior cord.

questions.s: The long thoracic nerve:
o: Is formed by C5 and C6 roots passing through scalenus medius, joined by C7 which descends in front of the muscle

Last's describes the long thoracic nerve formed by C5 and C6 roots passing through scalenus medius, joined by C7 which descends in front of the muscle.
The nerve then runs down into the axilla.
Runs down behind the midaxillary line on the surface of serratus anterior

The long thoracic nerve runs down behind the midaxillary line on the surface of serratus anterior, so it lies behind the lateral cutaneous branches of the intercostals and is safe from a midaxillary incision placed in front of it.
It is at risk in axillary dissection.
Supplies serratus anterior segmentally, with C7 to the lowest four digitations

It supplies serratus anterior segmentally: C5 to the upper two digitations, C6 to the next two, C7 to the lowest four.
Injury causes winging of the scapula.
Passes in front of the roots of the brachial plexus

The dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves pass behind the roots of the plexus. The nerve to subclavius passes in front of them.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.

questions.s: Concerning the axillary artery:
o: It is divided into three parts by pectoralis minor

The axillary artery is divided into three parts by pectoralis minor: first part above, second behind and third below.
The parts have one, two and three branches.
The superior thoracic artery arises from the first part

The superior thoracic artery is the single branch of the first part.
It supplies the upper chest wall.
The lateral thoracic artery arises from the third part

The lateral thoracic and thoracoacromial arteries arise from the second part, not the third.
The third gives the subscapular and two circumflex humeral arteries.
It becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major

The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major.
A landmark for brachial artery exposure.

questions.s: Structures piercing the clavipectoral fascia include the:
o: Cephalic vein

The cephalic vein pierces the clavipectoral fascia to reach the axillary vein. Mnemonic CALL: cephalic vein, acromiothoracic artery, lateral pectoral nerve, lymphatics.
These pierce it.
Medial pectoral nerve

The medial pectoral nerve pierces pectoralis minor, not the clavipectoral fascia.
Confusingly, it lies lateral to the lateral pectoral nerve.
Lateral thoracic artery

The lateral thoracic artery follows the lower border of pectoralis minor and does not pierce the clavipectoral fascia.
It supplies the lateral chest wall and breast.
Long thoracic nerve

The long thoracic nerve runs on the surface of serratus anterior, nowhere near the clavipectoral fascia.
Answer A: 1 only.

questions.s: Regarding the spaces of the posterior axillary wall:
o: The quadrangular space transmits the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels

The quadrangular space transmits the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels. It is bounded by teres minor above, teres major below, the long head of triceps medially and the humerus laterally.
Shoulder dislocation can stretch the nerve here.
In the quadrangular space the axillary nerve lies below the vessels

Last's says in the quadrangular space the axillary nerve lies above the vessels, in contact with the surgical neck just below the capsule.
So fractures of the surgical neck damage it.
The triangular space (interval) transmits the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels

The lower triangular space (interval) transmits the radial nerve and the profunda brachii vessels. It is bounded by teres major above, the long head of triceps medially and the humerus laterally.
The radial nerve then enters the spiral groove.
The circumflex scapular artery passes through the space bounded by teres minor, teres major and the long head of triceps

The circumflex scapular artery passes through the upper triangular space, bounded by teres minor, teres major and the long head of triceps, medial to the long head.
The quadrangular space lies lateral to the long head.

questions.s: The axillary nerve:
o: Supplies teres major

Teres major is supplied by the lower subscapular nerve, not the axillary nerve.
The axillary supplies teres minor.
Supplies teres minor through its posterior branch

The posterior branch of the axillary nerve supplies teres minor and part of deltoid, then becomes the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm.
The anterior branch supplies the rest of deltoid.
Supplies the skin of the back of the arm down to the elbow

The skin of the back of the arm down to the elbow is supplied by the posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm (radial). The axillary nerve supplies the skin over the lower half of deltoid ("regimental badge" area).
That patch is tested after shoulder dislocation.
Supplies the shoulder joint

The axillary nerve gives an articular branch to the shoulder joint.
Hilton's law again. Answer B: 2 and 4.

questions.s: Concerning the musculocutaneous nerve:
o: It pierces coracobrachialis

The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis, then slopes down between biceps and brachialis.
It supplies all three.
It supplies the lateral part of brachialis

The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the main part of brachialis. The lateral part, developed in the extensor compartment, is supplied by the radial nerve.
A dual supply.
It becomes the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm lateral to the biceps tendon

The musculocutaneous nerve becomes the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, piercing the deep fascia lateral to the biceps tendon at the elbow crease.
It supplies the lateral forearm skin.
Its root value is C5, C6 and C7

Its root value is C5, C6 and C7, from the lateral cord.
It is the nerve of the flexor compartment of the arm.

questions.s: Within the cubital fossa:
o: The median nerve lies medial to the brachial artery

In the cubital fossa, from medial to lateral, lie the median nerve, the brachial artery and the biceps tendon. So the median nerve lies medial to the artery.
The artery divides at the apex.
The ulnar nerve lies medial to the median nerve

Last's says the ulnar nerve does not run in the cubital fossa; it passes behind the medial epicondyle.
It enters the forearm through the cubital tunnel.
The bicipital aponeurosis separates the median cubital vein from the brachial artery

The bicipital aponeurosis separates the median cubital vein (superficial) from the brachial artery and median nerve (deep).
It protects them during venepuncture.
The radial nerve lies in the floor on supinator

The radial nerve lies just lateral to the cubital fossa, in the slit between brachialis and brachioradialis, not in the floor on supinator.
It divides there into superficial and deep branches.

questions.s: Regarding the median nerve:
o: It gives no muscular branches in the arm

The median nerve gives no muscular branches in the arm, unless the branch to pronator teres arises unusually high.
It gives branches in the forearm and hand.
It enters the forearm between the two heads of pronator teres

The median nerve enters the forearm between the two heads of pronator teres. The ulnar head of pronator teres separates it from the ulnar artery.
A site of compression (pronator syndrome).
Its palmar cutaneous branch passes deep to the flexor retinaculum

The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises just above the flexor retinaculum and passes superficial to it, so it is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.
Sensation over the thenar eminence is preserved.
It divides into its branches within the carpal tunnel

Last's says the median nerve divides into its branches (lateral with the recurrent motor branch, and medial) within the carpal tunnel.
The recurrent branch is at risk in carpal tunnel release.

questions.s: The anterior interosseous nerve supplies:
o: Flexor pollicis longus

The anterior interosseous nerve supplies flexor pollicis longus, one of the deep flexor compartment muscles.
With the lateral half of FDP and pronator quadratus.
The wrist and carpal joints

Last's says the anterior interosseous nerve also supplies the wrist and carpal joints, the interosseous membrane and periosteum.
It is a mixed nerve with articular fibres.
Pronator quadratus

The anterior interosseous nerve ends in pronator quadratus.
It runs on the interosseous membrane.
The lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus

It supplies the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus (to the index and middle fingers).
Its palsy causes inability to make an "OK" sign. All four true: E.

questions.s: Concerning the flexor retinaculum and carpal tunnel:
o: The retinaculum is attached to the pisiform and hook of hamate medially

The flexor retinaculum is attached medially to the pisiform and hook of hamate, and laterally to the tubercle of scaphoid and ridge of trapezium.
It roofs the carpal tunnel.
The median nerve lies lateral to the tendons of FDS and medial to FCR

In the carpal tunnel the median nerve lies just beneath the retinaculum, lateral to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis and medial to flexor carpi radialis, above FPL and FDP.
It is the most superficial structure.
The ulnar nerve passes through the carpal tunnel

The ulnar nerve and artery pass superficial to the flexor retinaculum, lateral to the pisiform, in Guyon's canal.
So carpal tunnel syndrome spares the ulnar nerve.
Flexor pollicis brevis has the most variable nerve supply of any muscle

Last's says flexor pollicis brevis has the most variable nerve supply of any muscle: the median recurrent branch, the deep ulnar branch, or both.
So thenar wasting may be incomplete in median palsy.

questions.s: Regarding the ulnar nerve:
o: It gives no branches in the arm

The ulnar nerve gives no branches in the arm; its first branches are at the elbow.
Like the median nerve.
It pierces the medial intermuscular septum in the lower third of the arm

The ulnar nerve pierces the medial intermuscular septum in the lower third of the arm, with the superior ulnar collateral artery and the radial nerve branch to the medial head of triceps.
It then passes behind the medial epicondyle.
It enters the forearm between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris

The ulnar nerve enters the forearm between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, through the cubital tunnel.
A common site of entrapment.
It divides into superficial and deep branches proximal to the wrist crease

The ulnar nerve divides into superficial and deep branches on the flexor retinaculum, beside the pisiform. The dorsal branch arises proximal to the wrist.
So a wrist laceration spares dorsal sensation.

questions.s: The deep branch of the ulnar nerve supplies:
o: Adductor pollicis

The deep branch of the ulnar nerve ends by supplying adductor pollicis.
So ulnar palsy causes Froment's sign.
All the interossei

The deep branch supplies all the interossei, palmar and dorsal.
Hence weakness of finger abduction and adduction.
The two medial lumbricals

The deep branch supplies the third and fourth (medial two) lumbricals.
The lateral two are median.
The hypothenar muscles

The deep branch passes between flexor and abductor digiti minimi and through opponens digiti minimi, supplying all three hypothenar muscles.
All four true: E.

questions.s: Concerning the radial nerve:
o: It gives a branch to the medial head of triceps in the axilla (the ulnar collateral nerve)

The radial nerve gives a branch to the medial head of triceps in the axilla, the ulnar collateral nerve, which runs with the ulnar nerve.
So high radial lesions can still spare part of triceps.
The posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm arises before the nerve enters the spiral groove

The posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm arises from the radial nerve in the axilla, before it enters the spiral groove.
It supplies the back of the arm.
It enters the anterior compartment by piercing the lateral intermuscular septum

The radial nerve enters the anterior compartment by piercing the lateral intermuscular septum, then lies between brachialis and brachioradialis.
It is exposed here in surgery.
It supplies extensor carpi radialis brevis before dividing

Last's says the radial nerve supplies brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus, then gives the posterior interosseous nerve, which supplies ECRB and supinator.
ECRB is supplied after the division.

questions.s: Following division of the superficial branch of the radial nerve at the wrist:
o: There is wrist drop

The superficial branch of the radial nerve is purely sensory, so its division causes no wrist drop.
Wrist drop needs a lesion of the main radial nerve above the elbow.
Sensory loss is often confined to a small area over the first dorsal interosseous

Last's says the sensory loss is often confined to a small area over the first dorsal interosseous, because of overlap from the median and ulnar nerves.
The autonomous zone is small.
There is weakness of extensor pollicis longus

Extensor pollicis longus is supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve, so it is not weakened.
The superficial branch has no motor fibres.
Sensory loss usually involves the anatomical snuffbox

Cutaneous branches cross the snuffbox tendons, so sensory loss usually involves the skin of the anatomical snuffbox.
They can be injured in de Quervain's release. Answer B: 2 and 4.

questions.s: The anatomical snuffbox:
o: Is bounded medially by extensor pollicis longus

The anatomical snuffbox is bounded medially (dorsally) by extensor pollicis longus and laterally by extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus.
It is visible when the thumb is extended.
Has the scaphoid and trapezium in its floor

The floor of the snuffbox contains the scaphoid and trapezium, with the radial styloid proximally.
Tenderness here suggests a scaphoid fracture.
Contains the radial artery

The radial artery crosses the floor of the snuffbox, deep to the tendons.
Its pulse can be felt there.
Contains the posterior interosseous nerve

The posterior interosseous nerve does not lie in the snuffbox. The cephalic vein begins there and branches of the superficial radial nerve cross it.
The PIN ends at the back of the wrist joint.

questions.s: Concerning the shoulder region muscles and nerves:
o: The suprascapular nerve passes below the superior transverse scapular ligament

The suprascapular nerve passes below the superior transverse scapular ligament, through the suprascapular notch; the vessels pass above it.
"Army goes over the bridge, navy goes under."
The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus

The suprascapular nerve (C5, C6 from the upper trunk) supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
It can be entrapped at the notch.
Subscapularis is supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves

Subscapularis is supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves; the lower also supplies teres major.
Both from the posterior cord.
Teres minor is supplied by the suprascapular nerve

Teres minor is supplied by the axillary nerve, not the suprascapular nerve.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.

questions.s: Regarding the segmental supply of upper limb movements:
o: Shoulder abduction and lateral rotation are C5

Shoulder abduction and lateral rotation are C5. Adduction and medial rotation are C6 to C8.
C5 is the "shoulder root".
Elbow flexion is C5 and C6

Elbow flexion is C5 and C6; elbow extension is C7 and C8.
Biceps reflex C5/6, triceps C7.
Forearm pronation is C6

Forearm supination is C6; pronation is C7 and C8.
"Supinate six."
The intrinsic muscles of the hand are T1

The intrinsic muscles of the hand are T1; abductor pollicis brevis is a key T1 test.
T1 root lesions waste the hand.

questions.s: Regarding the upper limb dermatomes and axial lines:
o: The anterior axial line runs from the sternal angle down the front of the limb almost to the wrist

The anterior axial line runs from the sternal angle down the front of the limb almost to the wrist; there is no overlap across it.
It separates C5/C6 from C8/T1 territories.
C7 supplies the middle finger

C7 supplies the middle finger. C6 supplies the thumb (and probably index), C8 the ring and little fingers.
Useful in radiculopathy.
The posterior axial line runs from the vertebra prominens to the insertion of deltoid

The posterior axial line runs from the vertebra prominens across the back and down the arm to the insertion of deltoid.
A second axial line on the back of the limb.
T1 supplies the skin of the axilla

Last's says T1 supplies the medial side of the elbow region, not the axilla. T2 supplies the axilla.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.

questions.s: Following an upper trunk (C5, C6) brachial plexus injury:
o: The arm hangs medially rotated at the side

Loss of deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor makes the arm hang medially rotated at the side: the waiter's tip posture (Erb's palsy).
Classic after birth injury or a fall on the shoulder.
Elbow flexion is weak

Elbow flexion is weak because biceps, brachialis and brachioradialis are C5 and C6.
The forearm is pronated too.
There is a sensory deficit over the lateral arm and forearm

There is sensory loss over the lateral arm and forearm (C5 and C6 dermatomes).
Including the regimental badge area.
The biceps jerk is preserved

The biceps jerk (C5, C6) is lost in an upper trunk lesion.
The triceps jerk is preserved.

questions.s: A lower trunk (C8, T1) lesion with avulsion of the T1 root would produce:
o: Ipsilateral Horner's syndrome

Preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the head leave in the T1 root, so T1 avulsion causes ipsilateral Horner's syndrome.
It suggests a preganglionic (root) lesion.
Wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles

T1 supplies the small muscles of the hand, so they waste (Klumpke's palsy, claw hand).
A lower trunk lesion.
Sensory loss on the medial forearm

There is sensory loss on the medial forearm and hand (C8 and T1 territory).
The medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm is T1.
Paralysis of deltoid

Deltoid is C5 and C6, so it is spared.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.

questions.s: Concerning arteries of the upper limb:
o: The subscapular artery continues as the thoracodorsal artery after giving the circumflex scapular

The subscapular artery gives the circumflex scapular artery, then continues as the thoracodorsal artery down the posterior axillary wall.
It supplies latissimus dorsi (used in flaps).
The anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries arise from the third part of the axillary artery

The anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries arise from the third part of the axillary artery, with the subscapular.
Three branches from the third part.
The radial artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox

The radial artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox, then passes between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous into the palm.
It forms the deep palmar arch.
The deep palmar arch is formed mainly by the ulnar artery

The deep palmar arch is formed mainly by the radial artery. The superficial arch is mainly ulnar.
Allen's test checks both supplies.

questions.s: Regarding ossification in the upper limb:
o: The clavicle is the first bone in the body to ossify

The clavicle is the first bone in the body to ossify, in membrane from two centres in the fifth week.
It is also one of the last to fuse.
The capitate is the first carpal bone to ossify

The capitate is the first carpal bone to ossify (in the first year); the pisiform is last, at about 10 years.
Carpal ossification helps estimate bone age.
The medial epicondyle of the humerus fuses with the shaft separately at about 20 years

The medial epicondyle fuses with the shaft separately at about 20 years. The other three lower humeral centres fuse together, then with the shaft at about 15 years.
A displaced medial epicondyle can be trapped in the elbow joint.
The upper end of the radius is the growing end

The lower end of the radius is its growing end. In the upper limb the growing ends are at the shoulder and the wrist ("to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee").
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.

questions.s: Concerning the posterior interosseous nerve:
o: It passes between the two layers of supinator

The posterior interosseous nerve passes between the two layers of supinator, under the arcade of Frohse.
A site of entrapment.
It supplies all the muscles of the common extensor origin and the deep extensors

It supplies all the muscles of the common extensor origin and the deep extensors, including EPL, EPB, APL and extensor indicis.
So its palsy causes finger drop without wrist drop.
It ends by supplying the wrist joint

The posterior interosseous nerve ends by supplying the wrist joint, after running on the interosseous membrane.
Its terminal part can be resected for wrist pain.
It supplies brachioradialis

Brachioradialis is supplied by the radial nerve before its division, not by the posterior interosseous nerve.
So brachioradialis works in PIN palsy.

questions.s: The recurrent (muscular) branch of the median nerve usually supplies:
o: Adductor pollicis

Adductor pollicis is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve, not the median recurrent branch.
It is the ulnar nerve's last muscle.
First dorsal interosseous

All the interossei, including the first dorsal interosseous, are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
Its wasting shows on the dorsum of the first web.
Palmaris brevis

Palmaris brevis is supplied by the superficial branch of the ulnar nerve.
It is the only muscle supplied by that branch.
Abductor pollicis brevis

The recurrent branch of the median nerve curves around the distal border of the flexor retinaculum to supply the thenar muscles, including abductor pollicis brevis.
Answer D: 4 only.

questions.s: Regarding the lumbricals and interossei:
o: The lumbricals arise from the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus

The lumbricals arise from the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus and insert into the radial side of the extensor expansions.
They link flexor and extensor systems.
The lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints

The lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints. Their paralysis causes the claw deformity.
Hyperextended MCPs, flexed IPs.
The dorsal interossei adduct the fingers

The dorsal interossei abduct the fingers (DAB); the palmar interossei adduct them (PAD).
"PAD and DAB."
The first and second lumbricals are usually supplied by the median nerve

The first and second (lateral) lumbricals are usually supplied by the median nerve; the third and fourth by the deep ulnar nerve.
So clawing is worse in the ring and little fingers in ulnar palsy.
